questions.q: Why can't you join any two Salesforce objects in a report the way you can join any two tables in T-SQL?
options: Reports must be built on a report type, which is a fixed path through related objects
Salesforce reports never support more than one object
Joins are only allowed in dashboards, not reports
Custom objects cannot be reported on at all
questions.explain: Every report starts from a report type that defines which objects and relationships are available. Cross filters and joined reports stretch this but do not provide free joins.

questions.q: What is the safest way to handle a specific limit number, such as how many rows a report page displays?
options: Quote the number from memory as a permanent fact
Describe it in general terms and check current Salesforce documentation, since limits change by release and edition
Assume the limit is identical in every org forever
Ignore limits until a report fails
questions.explain: Limits vary by edition and change over time, so describe them generally and verify against current documentation before promising anything.

questions.q: A stakeholder wants pipeline as it stood on the first day of each quarter for two years, and no history was ever captured. What is true?
options: A standard report can recreate it by changing the date filter
A dashboard filter will retrieve the old values
Standard reports show current data, and snapshots or trend reporting must be set up in advance to capture history
Salesforce automatically stores every historical value of every field for reports
questions.explain: A standard report shows records as they are now. Reporting snapshots and historical trend reports help, but only from the point you set them up.

questions.q: Which request most clearly falls outside what native reports can do?
options: Opportunity amount grouped by stage
Cases opened this month grouped by priority
Combining Salesforce opportunities with revenue from an external ERP in one analysis
Filtering leads by lead source
questions.explain: Native reports can only use data that lives in Salesforce. Blending in outside systems needs another tool or a data load.

questions.q: Why can very large objects with broad filters make native reports slow?
options: Reports query live transactional data, so volume and filter design affect run time
Reports are stored as static PDFs
Salesforce blocks reports on objects with over 100 records
Dashboards are always slower than reports by design
questions.explain: Reports run against live data, so large objects, weak filters, and complex cross filters can be slow or time out.
